rv.q: Particularly when Parsons or Hecht is onstage, Harvey is a sweet treat.

Such is the charm of the director Scott Ellis's production of this 1944 chestnut, led by a supremely winning Jim Parsons as the gentle protagonist, Elwood P. Dowd, that you may find yourself wistfully scanning the departing crowds for a glimpse of Elwood's boon companion.
The nuttier the farce becomes, in fact, the better this show is.
So is any real reason to see it.
He is so convincing in his give-and-take with Harvey that we almost begin to see the mischievous sprite.
It's good and often silly fun, greatly enriched by Parson's performance.
As a gentle ode to acceptance and nonconformity, “Harvey” is enjoyable — no more, no less.

It's thin stuff and difficult to pull off because a lot of the action happens offstage and is merely recounted, but this production has moments, while not really soaring into the absurdist yet warming stratosphere.
Alas, the same might be said of Scott Ellis' oddly sluggish production, which lurches from scene to scene when it should be bunny-hopping briskly along.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this revival, with Jim Parsons earning praise for his charming, well-suited performance as Elwood, though some find the production uneven or dull overall.
